idiom_name: duck-typed policy object (class, instance or function) passed to the host
implementation_notes: Python's policy unit is whatever object implements the expected protocol - a class, an instance, a module or a plain function - passed to the host's constructor and stored on it; typing.Protocol (PEP 544) documents the contract for static checkers while abc.ABC or @runtime_checkable can enforce it at run time. Structure-building policies are usually delegated to the standard library (sorted(key=...), collections.abc, functools) instead of a policy class, so the classic host+policy-class hierarchy is replaced by composition plus one explicit constructor parameter. Reach for mixins/ABCs when the host itself must expose the policy's methods, and use PEP 695 type parameters only to document the binding - the run-time realization does not change.
pitfalls: Protocols are checked only by static analysis: at run time a missing method raises AttributeError when the policy is first used, so validate external policies once in __init__.
A default policy built in the signature (def __init__(self, policy=LruPolicy())) is created once and shared by every host constructed without one - build it per instance instead.
Because conformance is structural, a class with a coincidentally named method satisfies the protocol; keep policy contracts narrow and explicitly typed to avoid accidental matches.
